records.content: Scientific actions are exposed under stable public names. Every command in this notebook runs on the Dear PyGui thread, writes only documented controls and invokes the callback already used by the graphical interface. The command layer does not contain a second PTU, ROI, filtering or concentration implementation.

A client sends a public command such as phot2conc.set_calibration. The adapter validates its scientific arguments, writes the corresponding calibration controls, invokes callback_omega_input, callback_kappa_input, and the existing brightness callbacks, then returns normalized state. Widget tags and Python callback names remain private implementation details.

Operation order remains under client control. Select the mode first, load a directory, set controls, and then request calculation or export. OPERATION_UNAVAILABLE means that the requested mode or prerequisite GUI state is missing. INVALID_PARAMETERS identifies malformed public arguments.

The library/filter commands use explicit parameters: extract.set_background_range requires channel and enabled; extract.open_decay_library and extract.import_library_decays require channel; extract.select_library_decay and extract.select_filter require channel and the exact displayed name. Channels accept 1 or 2. Missing prerequisites return OPERATION_UNAVAILABLE together with available decay or filter names where applicable.

smica-call phot2conc.load_directory '{"directory":"/absolute/data/path"}'
smica-call phot2conc.load_calibration '{"path":"/absolute/path/to/calib.json"}'
smica-call phot2conc.set_roi_source '{"source":"auto"}'
smica-call phot2conc.set_auto_roi '{"channel":1,"cell_threshold":0.85,"many_cells":false}'
smica-call phot2conc.calculate '{}'
smica-call phot2conc.add_result '{}'
smica-call phot2conc.export_results '{"path":"/absolute/output/results.csv"}'

The client can send the sequence one command at a time or from a shell/Python workflow. Article workflows use the same public commands, preserve resume state and finish with a concise processing report.

Statistical-filter automation follows the existing GUI flow. Enable filtering, initialize the setup for a channel and either enable automatic background selection or import a compatible decay from the library. Calculate and accept the filter, select the accepted foreground filter, and then execute the native batch callback. The automation handlers pass the real sender tags and callback arguments used by the corresponding controls.

For a saved decay pattern, use this order:

extract.set_statistical_filter

extract.open_filter_setup

extract.calculate_filters to initialise the filtering window

extract.open_decay_library

extract.select_library_decay

extract.import_library_decays

Select the imported row and run extract.calculate_filters again

extract.accept_filters

extract.select_filter

extract.apply_all

The filter calculation checks that a decay component or automatic background range is selected. Import also preserves the GUI compatibility check between the current PTU and library decay TCSPC channel counts. extract.apply_all refuses to start when statistical filtering is enabled, but no foreground filter has been selected for an active channel.

Tests use instrumented Dear PyGui and mode objects to verify ordering at the interaction boundary: widget values are written and the same callback methods used by GUI controls are invoked. Covered paths include initial-button mode transition, decay gating, filter-window initialization, automatic background selection, decay-library import, foreground-filter selection, calibration, automatic ROI controls and Phot2conc calculation.

The repository defines 58 pytest test functions covering the protocol, registry, dispatcher, TCP client/server, panel, callback parity and PTU reader/router. The installed --test runner additionally executes four readable numerical scripts for frame reconstruction, concentration formulas, ROI masks and weighted lifetime calculations. Native Apply to all and Calculate all callbacks retain GUI progress reporting. Error responses identify the failed public command in both the message and details.command.

Numerical compatibility is evaluated through explicit expected-versus-calculated values and documented tolerances. Long workflows also report completed, skipped and reused batches so interrupted work can be resumed without repeating accepted results. These checks complement manual GUI parity; representative measurements are still required when adding a new PTU hardware backend or scanner type.

Status: implemented in v2.2.0. This notebook records the current command boundary, scientific-operation coverage, hidden state, protocol contracts and reproducibility policy. The TCP layer reuses existing GUI callbacks and does not introduce a parallel scientific calculation engine.

The transport uses loopback TCP, newline-delimited JSON, an explicit command registry and a thread-safe queue consumed on the GUI thread.

The initial design audit has been retained as implementation rationale, while the tables below describe the current v2.2.0 interface. Commands for extraction, statistical-filter setup, filter-library import, foreground-filter selection, Phot2conc calculation and export are operational. Complete publication workflows are currently orchestrated by scripts that call this public interface and maintain their own resume/report state.

Manual and automated PTU-to-concentration paths use the same native batch callbacks.

The GUI remains the source of truth for workflow order and scientific execution. Public commands use stable scientific names rather than exposing arbitrary widget tags, but their handlers set the corresponding Dear PyGui values and invoke existing callbacks on the GUI thread. A user or workflow script defines the same operation sequence that would be performed interactively.

Validated commands bind to existing widgets, callbacks, mode objects and result attributes. Small adapters are used only when an existing callback needs deterministic arguments, normally relies on an interactive file dialog or does not expose a machine-readable result. Numerical code remains in its established execution path.

Scientific operations include PTU decoding, raster reconstruction, frame integration, decay gating, statistical-filter calculation and application, ROI construction, effective-volume calculation, photon-to-molecule conversion, concentration calculation, uncertainty calculation and numerical export. Pure presentation settings remain outside the workflow unless they change a scientific selection.

The live system.capabilities response is the authoritative command inventory. Background-range control, decay-library selection/import and foreground-filter selection are fully represented by public commands. Batch execution calls the native GUI methods so file-specific data are refreshed and progress remains visible. Frame-wise products are stored in PKL and appended during table export rather than being represented as independent TCP commands.

Family

Purpose

Health, version and live command capabilities.

High-level application and mounted-mode state.

Arbitrary widget access is deliberately not public. The exact commands and descriptions are returned by system.capabilities.

Protocol version 1 uses one UTF-8 JSON object per line. Every request carries protocol_version, a client-supplied request_id, a registered command and an object-valued parameters member. Authentication is optional and is not returned in logs or responses. Responses echo the request ID and contain either a result or a stable error object.

The normal launcher accepts --automation-server, --automation-port and timeout/queue options. The server can also be started and stopped from the About > Automation server panel. It binds to 127.0.0.1, applies bounded request and queue limits and never executes Dear PyGui calls on the socket thread.

Machine-readable request and response schemas are stored in src/smICA/res/schemas/automation_request_v1.schema.json and automation_response_v1.schema.json. Command validators reject unknown fields and normalize accepted parameters before dispatch.

The article workflow is an external shell orchestrator that sends validated public commands to one running smICA instance. Dataset order is deterministic. Calibration values for dextran measurements are selected using both the acquisition-date directory and excitation-power directory; the selected JSON supplies the numerical calibration fields sent to Phot2conc.

Automatic ROI selection uses foreground intensity. File-based workflows enumerate ROI names associated with each measurement. Output reuse is controlled by explicit resume state and by checking that the expected completed output is present. Scientific commands continue to use the active GUI state and native callbacks.

Extraction configures gates and statistical filters once for a compatible directory and then calls Apply to all. Phot2conc loads calibration and ROI state and calls Calculate all, including every matching ROI. The workflow can restrict execution to selected dataset families, for example mRNA measurements only. Completed extraction/calculation batches are recorded in a resume-state file and skipped on restart. At termination, the report records success or failure, input and processed counts, reused/skipped counts, elapsed time, host, operating system, kernel, CPU, logical CPU count, memory and Python version.

The workflow report records the smICA workflow status, start and finish timestamps, elapsed time, input PTU count, successful extraction/calculation batches, skipped or reused batches, exported result-file and row counts, the resume-state location and machine specification. Result tables retain measurement, ROI and channel identifiers together with integrated and available frame-resolved numerical fields. Authentication data are never included.

The migration fixture set covers Standard and PIE acquisitions, 128×128 and 256×256 rasters, single- and dual-detector data, and short and long frame series. Validation uses:

Exact invariants: metadata, integer photon/marker/frame counts, shapes, selected frame sums, masks when deterministic and file ordering.

Floating-point invariants: effective volume, molecules, concentration, uncertainty terms, decay maps and statistical-filter arrays with documented absolute and relative tolerances.

Structural invariants: output naming, report status, warnings, per-file failures and resume behaviour.

The historical reader preserves the known earlier effective-frame interpretation only for compatibility with older PKL files. Corrected PicoHarp validation relies on decoded routed-photon totals, marker-derived frame boundaries, agreement between frame sums and the integrated image, analytical numerical examples and manual GUI parity. Current real fixtures do not cover malformed marker streams, missing frames, T2 records, every PicoQuant record type or every scanner; unsupported combinations remain on the explicit legacy route or fail validation.

Reproducibility records use input/output names, sizes, effective parameters, software versions, processing status, warnings, failures, resume state and quantitative summaries. The workflow does not generate or verify checksum files. Scientific agreement is assessed from explicit numerical invariants and tolerances rather than file digests.

Pure layout controls, display contrast/brightness, ROI-overlay opacity, colour-map display ranges, help windows and file-dialog navigation are intentionally outside the scientific API. Standalone Rewrite ROI and ROI Mixer operations are documented as preparatory tools and are not part of the automated PTU-to-concentration path. Writing new shared filter-library entries is also not exposed because it changes persistent application resources and requires an explicit collision policy. Unsupported reader/backend combinations fail validation instead of silently switching frame semantics.

The entry point, scientific modes, common state, packaging and user notebooks have been audited.

The documented PTU extraction, filtering, calibration, ROI, calculation, export and native batch paths have public commands.

Commands execute on the GUI thread and reuse existing callbacks.

Version-2 PKL output contains integrated and frame-resolved products.

Installed numerical tests report expected and calculated values.

Article workflows support resume state and final processing reports.

New PTU hardware/scanner combinations still require representative fixtures and independent numerical validation before support is claimed.

smICA v2.2.0 provides an optional versioned TCP/JSON interface for scripted operation. The normal graphical application still starts with the server disabled. Infrastructure and scientific commands are registered in the same running application, and scientific work is dispatched to the Dear PyGui thread.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

Start the installed application with run_smICA --automation-server on Linux or smICA.bat --automation-server on Windows. The listener binds only to 127.0.0.1; the default port is 8765 and can be changed with --automation-port. The About > Automation server panel reports whether the listener is running and displays the effective local address. Commands are sent by the installed smica-call client from another terminal on the same machine.

Start the ordinary graphical application:run_smICA

Start smICA with the automation server immediately enabled:run_smICA --automation-server --automation-port 8765

Port 0 selects a free port. --automation-print-startup prints a one-line JSON startup record containing the effective port:run_smICA --automation-server --automation-port 0 --automation-print-startup

The same server can be started or stopped after launch from About → Automation server. The panel displays status, loopback address, and effective port. It never displays an authentication token.

For a remote-shell workflow, log in to the remote account, start smICA with the option above, and run the client from another shell on the same machine.

The installer provides both smica-call and smica_call as text-based Bash scripts on Linux and Batch scripts on Windows. No compiled automation-client launcher is installed. Send a readiness request with:smica-call --port 8765 system.health

Send a command with a JSON parameter object:smica-call --port 8765 command.name '{"parameter": "value"}'

Exit status is 0 for a successful server response, 1 for a command error returned by smICA, and 2 for local validation or connection failure.

Authentication is optional for same-account local operation. Supply a token to smICA through SMICA_AUTOMATION_TOKEN or through --automation-token-file. The client reads the same environment variable or accepts --token-file. A token is never required as a command-line literal and is not included in normal logs, status output, or result manifests.SMICA_AUTOMATION_TOKEN="$(cat token.txt)" \
  run_smICA --automation-server

smica-call --token-file token.txt system.health

Command

Purpose

system.health

Confirm readiness and report the effective listener state.

system.version

Report application and protocol versions.

system.capabilities

Return sorted metadata for the current explicit command allowlist.

session.inspect

Return high-level GUI session state without exposing widget identifiers.

system.shutdown

Available only when smICA starts with --automation-allow-shutdown; intended for controlled tests.

No command exposes Python evaluation, dynamic import, unrestricted object access, arbitrary widget mutation, or unrestricted file-system operations.

Documentation added for v2.2.0

Run smica-call system.capabilities '{}' against the active application to obtain the authoritative, version-specific command list. The result includes every public command name, description and GUI-thread requirement. Human-readable command groups and examples are maintained in 

Automation commands, but scripts should use the live capability response when validating availability.

The socket listener runs in a background thread. It validates and authenticates requests, then places them in a bounded queue. The controlled Dear PyGui render loop processes a limited number per frame on the GUI thread. The transport thread never calls Dear PyGui.

Stopping the server closes the listener while leaving the application and dispatcher available for a later manual restart. Closing smICA stops the listener, cancels queued requests, stops the documentation server, and destroys the Dear PyGui context. Server startup and shutdown are idempotent.

The non-interactive suite covers protocol encoding and validation, duplicate command rejection, parameter validation, queue saturation, cancellation, local error redaction, execution-thread identity, fragmented requests, multiple requests per connection, malformed traffic, request limits, authentication, concurrent clients, operation timeout, client disconnect, graceful listener shutdown, client exit behaviour and real Dear PyGui panel creation.

The server starts disabled when no automation option is supplied. Linux and Windows launchers forward optional arguments. Every Dear PyGui item added by the automation panel has an explicit tag and is registered in globalITEMS.items so ordinary mode switching remains safe.

smICA analytical methods are directory-based add-ons. Each complete method placed in src/smICA/Modes is discovered at startup and added to the Analysis menu. The built-in Extract_from_PTU and Phot2conc methods use the same mechanism as additional methods.

Copy the complete templates/add_on_template directory to src/smICA/Modes.

Rename the copied directory to a short, import-safe method name.

Rename the files and replace every Template and template identifier, including import paths, class names, callback names, mode paths, Dear PyGui tags, and visible labels.

Keep the method self-contained inside its directory. Shared, generally useful code may be placed under src/smICA/Required only when it is intentionally part of the application API.

Start smICA from a source checkout and confirm that the new entry appears in the Analysis menu, mounts correctly, resizes, and can be replaced by each other mode without leaving widgets behind.

The template is executable after it is copied without renaming, but all identifiers must be made unique before another add-on is introduced.

A mode directory is accepted only when it contains __init__.py, exactly one *_config.json file, and all three Python files named by that configuration. The configuration has four required string fields:{
  "LAYOUT": "MyMethod_layout.py",
  "INIT": "MyMethod_INIT.py",
  "ANAL_MENU_ITEM": "MyMethod_menu_item.py",
  "menu_class_func": "MyMethod_menu_F"
}

The filenames must be local basenames rather than absolute paths or paths containing parent-directory components. An incomplete or malformed method is ignored, which prevents a partially copied add-on from breaking application startup.

The *_menu_item.py file creates one item under menu_analysis_method_dropout. Its controller unmounts the active mode, sets inV.mounted_method, executes the selected layout, and connects mode-specific File-menu callbacks.

The *_layout.py file creates Dear PyGui windows and widgets. Every created item that must disappear while switching methods must be appended to globalITEMS.windows. It also installs the method’s resize callback.

The *_INIT.py file owns layout geometry, state, callbacks, validation, and analytical functions. Keeping calculations outside the layout declarations makes them easier to test.

The config file connects these entry points without requiring edits to the central application launcher.

Dear PyGui tags are application-global. Prefix every tag with the method name. Delete owned items in reverse creation order, reset the viewport resize callback when unmounting, and never add the Analysis-menu selector itself to globalITEMS.windows.

Separate file loading, numerical calculations, GUI updates, and exports into small functions. Numerical functions should accept arrays or plain Python values and return results without reading widget state internally; callbacks can translate GUI values into those inputs. Validate dimensionality, units, empty selections, NaN values, and incompatible channel metadata before starting a long calculation. Use os.path for filesystem paths so the method works on Linux and Windows.

Add required third-party libraries to the main project dependency definition. An updater can install code distributed by the official repository, but an add-on must not download or execute an undeclared dependency by itself.

During an official update, smICA scans src/smICA/Modes in the downloaded repository. Every complete mode is copied into the installed application’s Modes directory. Existing official modes are updated and new official add-ons are installed. Local mode directories that are absent from the repository are preserved; the synchronizer does not delete them. Incomplete repository mode directories are skipped and reported in the local update output. Restart smICA after an update so discovery runs again.

Add-ons execute Python code inside the smICA process and have the same filesystem permissions as the application. Install only trusted add-ons and review their source before copying them into Modes.

Add repository-level numerical and lifecycle tests under dev_tests; do not place developer-only tests in the installed calculation-test suite. At minimum, test calculation functions independently, missing or invalid input handling, mounting and unmounting, mode switching, resizing, and Linux/Windows path handling. Run the developer suite from the repository root with:python dev_tests/run_tests.py

If a method must be controlled through the TCP server, register narrowly scoped public commands in the automation command layer. A command should call the same callback path as the matching GUI action, validate its preconditions before changing state, return JSON-compatible results, and expose no arbitrary Python execution or unrestricted filesystem operation. Document each public command in the automation command reference.

The directory passes the required config contract and is discovered in deterministic order.

All files use the project MIT header and all source comments and identifiers are in English.

GUI tags, classes, callbacks, and menu objects are unique.

Switching to and from every installed mode removes all owned GUI items.

Long operations provide progress feedback and leave the GUI responsive.

Paths are built with os.path and have been checked on Linux and Windows.

Dependencies, user-facing behavior, outputs, and automation commands are documented.

python dev_tests/run_tests.py passes.

This tool is designed to perform a product, sum, or subtract operations on two ROI files generated with smICA.

From the Tool menu, select ROI mixer

It will open a new window that will help to navigate through the process,

Using the ROI1, ROI2 buttons define ROI files source to be used.

The ROI3 button defines the target ROI folder. The name of the resulting file will be the same as for ROI 1.

In the image fields below the buttons the ROI images will appear. First two represents ROI 1 and ROI 2. The third image is a result of operation on the first two ROIS.

In the middle of the window there is a drop down menu with available operations.

Press the Proceed button to save ROI 3 into file.

The ROI files created with this tool can be loaded directly into the smICA analysis workflow.

smICA v2.2.0 adds callback-backed TCP automation while retaining the same GUI calculation paths used during interactive analysis. PicoHarp 300 T3 files are decoded through phconvert. Version-2 PKL output stores integrated foreground, background, and fluorescence-lifetime maps, together with sparse, frame-resolved foreground and background data. Phot2conc displays the integrated image products and adds frame-resolved quantitative values only to exported tables. Phot2conc can also display the background image when filtering is applied and the fluorescence-decay-time image.

This repository provides software for calculating fluorophore concentrations from FLIM images stored in the PTU format (PicoQuant, Germany). The software allows the extraction of information about registered photons from the .ptu file, filtering them using statistical filters based on fluorescence decay time and autodetection of the region of interest (ROI), and finally creating a map of the absolute concentration of the fluorophore. The GUI is powered by 

Dear PyGui.

If you use the FcsIT software or any part of it in your academic work,
citation of the relevant publications listed below is appreciated.

Kalwarczyk et al. (2024)


Kalwarczyk (2026)

First, click “File” and “Open PTU directory” to select the folder storing your .ptu files.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

PicoHarp 300 T3 measurements are decoded by the phconvert backend. Raster markers are validated, photon coordinates are reconstructed, and every complete reconstructed frame is included in the integrated image. The output metadata identifies the reader backend and records the number of frame markers and the number of frames actually integrated. Unsupported PTU record types are routed explicitly to the readPTU_FLIM reader. Note that the readPTU_FLIM.py script miscounts the number of frames as N-1 due to the marker logic. Although the Phto2conc module displays N frames, it automatically applies the correction, and the output data are calculated for N-1 frames to maintain mathematical consistency. Unsupported or inconsistent data are reported rather than silently changing the frame semantics.



We suggest keeping the .ptu files for a single experiment in a dedicated folder, one folder per experiment. The lifetime analysis can be performed for each channel separately.

The main window of the method is composed of four sub-windows. If two detectors are used in the measurement, the signal will be automatically split and displayed as Channel 1 (red) and Channel 2 (green). The upper plots represent the whole signal acquired by a given detector. The lower plot displays only the parts of the signal selected by the draglines in the upper plots. The script recognises the measurement mode (standard or PIE). If the PIE mode is enabled, the draglines will automatically split the entire time range in half. Only the signal from the lower plots will be used for analysis.

Important! Some older hardware based on NIKON A1 and LSM upgrade kits from PicoQuant may experience a hardware communication bug between the A1 controller and the SymPhoTime software during .ptu file acquisition. Due to a bug, additional lines are added to the figure generated by SymPhoTime, resulting in a smeared appearance at the top of the figure. The panel marked with a yellow rectangle in the top-right corner of the main window lets you enable correction for additional lines.

The magenta rectangle marks the window containing all files from the selected folder, along with buttons to run the analysis for a single file or all files.
The software allows for two types of photon filtering. Each channel can be filtered independently.

The first filtering method uses simple time gating. It can be realised by selecting the region of interest in the fluorescence decay pattern by moving the orange and red drag lines displayed in the upper plots.

The second method is based on statistical TCSPC filtering, in which proper weights are assigned according to the procedure described in the literature (see 

Enderlein & Gregor (2005) and  

Kapusta et al. (2007)). Below is the step-by-step filtering procedure.

Checking the “Use statistical filters” checkbox under each channel deactivates draglines and activates

The “Calculate filters” opens a window (see below) where the user can calculate statistical filters for background or fluorescence decay patterns imported from the library.



On the left of the above window is a list of decay patterns. Initially, only one pattern appears, corresponding to the pattern extracted from the image at a given channel, the one from the plot.Selecting the “Set data range for background” checkbox activates draglines, allowing one to select the background region of the pattern, usually the plateau at the highest times of the decay pattern. Based on the selected region, the mean background signal is calculated and subtracted from the original decay data. The subtracted data is then used to calculate the statistical filter. altervnatively the filtering pattern can be 

stored in the library by pressing “To library”.

The background-free decay pattern can be stored in the library for later use. Press “To library”. To add the the pattern to the library.

The new fields will appear, which are required to store the data. Although some fields are optional, the more details you provide, the easier you will find the proper decay. To store the data, press “Submit”.

The previously stored decay data can also be imported by pressing the “Form library” button.

The new table will appear, containing all the stored decay patterns. Marking the decay and pressing “Import” will load the decay pattern.

For data imported from the library, the user needs to select the appropriate pattern required for the analysis. When only background removal is performed, it is recommended to select the “Remove afterpulsing” checkbox.

Pressing the “Calculate filters” button calculates weights, which are displayed in a new plot. Note that the calculations can take some time. The plot displays all the weights calculated for the curves in the left table, together with the background and afterpulsing signal.  To accept the current set of weights, press “Accept”; to reject and recalculate, press “Decline”.

The “Accept” button will close the window, and you can select the weights for analysis. Make sure you select the proper weights. For example, selecting the Afterpulsing and background weights will remove your fluorophore’s signal, and for the analysis, only the background signal will be used.

The same procedure can be repeated for Channel 2.

Finally, pressing one of the buttons labelled Apply to single PTU file or Apply to extract from all PTU files will run a filtering routine on a single selected file or on all files in the directory.

Apply to all is a native batch operation. The selected gate, line-correction setting and accepted foreground filter are defined once. During the batch, smICA selects every PTU in GUI order, reloads its current decay and image data, applies the configured procedure and updates the progress window. Each channel for which statistical filtering is enabled must have a foreground filter selected in the filter table before the batch starts. This prevents an incomplete configuration from producing partially filtered output.

Every time the filtering routine is applied, the script generates several files for further analysis. The files will be named after the used _ .ptu _ file.

The script will generate:

some-file.pkl  - The binary file containing experimental data. The file is necessary to generate the concentration map.

Two .png files per channel. One in the normalised grey scale and one in the false colours mode, where the intensity of fluorescence is mapped with different colours.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

Version-2 PKL files contain the integrated intensity_<channel>, bgrnd_<channel> and lifetimes_<channel> maps, reader metadata and frame_data_<channel>. Frame data use the sparse_frame_images_v1 representation: frame offsets identify events belonging to each frame, while pixel coordinates and foreground/background weights allow Phot2conc to reconstruct one image at a time without expanding the full stack in memory.

Foreground and background values after TCSPC filtering are weighted counts. They may be fractional because an event contributes according to its filter weight; they are not raw integer photon-event counts. The sum over reconstructed frames corresponds to the integrated weighted image for the same gate and filter configuration.

This mode allows for mapping the concentration of fluorescent molecules using single-molecule FLIM imaging data.
The script requires the .pkl files created in the 

EXTRACT from PTU and FILTER mode. Important! This script does not read the .ptu files directly. It is necessary to use the 

EXTRACT from PTU and FILTER mode first!

To open the folder containing the files for analysis, select Open PTU directory from the File menu. The directory may contain PTU files with their extracted PKL products. Historical PKL files remain readable; version-2 PKL files additionally provide integrated background/lifetime maps and sparse frame-resolved foreground/background data.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

Phot2conc accepts current PTU/PKL datasets and retains backward compatibility with older PKL data. Frame-resolved export columns are produced only when the loaded PKL contains frame_data_<channel> or the supported legacy frame arrays. Missing frame data do not change the integrated calculation.

The GUI is divided into several sections.

PTU metadata containing the information about image acquisition.

ROI containing the selection panel for choosing the method for the region of interest. It also allows control of the automatic ROI 

see below.

The list of files for analysis that are located in the PTU folder.

Buttons starting the calculations and export options.

Analysed image - 5’ for channel 1 and 5’’ for channel 2.

Histograms of the concentration number of molecules or number of photons per pixel - 6’ for channel 1 and 6’’ for channel 2.

The FCS calibration data

Mean results.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

The current interface also includes the display selector, which offers Foreground intensity, Background intensity, and Foreground decay times. Foreground intensity represents the weighted signal used for concentration calculation; background intensity represents the complementary TCSPC-weighted component; and foreground decay times show the weighted mean microtime converted to nanoseconds.

It is recommended to load or input the FCS calibration data and molecular brightness of the fluorophore, right after loading the 

PTU directory. Calibration data is obligatory for the proper calculation of the number of molecules and concentration. The calibration data can be loaded from the JSON files (exemplary files are stored in the 

samples folder on the repository site).
Alternatively, the calibration data can be entered manually by entering the correct values in the corresponding fields shown below.
The manually entered calibration values can be saved by pressing the Save calibration data button.

The analysed image is displayed in windows corresponding to channel 1, 2 or both.
Above the images, the user can adjust the visibility of the images by changing contrast and brightness, or the overlaying ROI’s alpha channel; 

see ROI section.

Note, the adjustment is applied only to the displayed image (channel 1 or channel 2) and does not affect the results.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

The DISPLAY OPTIONS selector switches between foreground intensity, TCSPC-weighted background intensity and foreground fluorescence-decay time. The three display products share the currently selected measurement and ROI state. Brightness/contrast controls and the minimum/maximum lifetime range modify presentation only; they do not alter the saved foreground values, ROI definition or quantitative result. Automatic ROI detection always segments the foreground-intensity image.

The background view reports weighted photon counts. Values can therefore be fractional after TCSPC filtering and should not be interpreted as raw integer photon events.

The decay-time view uses the colour scale and the visible minimum/maximum controls shown below each channel. These controls affect the displayed colour mapping only.

The region of interest, ROI, is a part of the image that will be considered during the image analysis. It is marked in red on the image. The software has two options for ROI definition: 

ROI from files or 

Auto ROI.

This option requires externally created roi files. Examples of externally generated ROI files (generated with ImageJ) are in the 

samples folder on the repository site. Before import, the externally created ROI files should be rewritten to a format readable by the smICA software with the 

REWRITE ROI tool.

Note that

The ROI file for each channel is created separately.

The filename of the ROI file should have the same structure as the PTU file with an additional string at the end of the filename, according to the example given below.file_name.ptufile_name_roi0_ch_1.dat - (ROI file for channel 1)file_name_roi0_ch_2.dat - (ROI file for channel 2)

The ROI files will load automatically for the given .ptu file. To import the ROI files, the user must specify the folder containing the files by selecting the path using the Open ROI directory option from the File menu. It is possible to have many ROI files per .ptu file. The multiple ROI files are identified by numeration in the roiX part of the ROI’s file name, where X denotes the number of the ROI file.

Selecting the Auto ROI checkbox displays the ROI control panel for both channels, and the ROI on the image as a red field.

Currently, the automatic ROI option offers:

automatic detection of a single cell,

automatic detection of more than one cell and selection of the ROI of interest (clicking on the image),

copying ROI between channels,

finding dark or bright areas,

subtracting dark or bright areas,

finding and subtracting many bright spots.

All modes use the OTSU thresholding method. The user can independently adjust the original OTSU threshold by changing the corresponding sliders in each channel.

ROI copying between channels is performed only in the “detect cell” mode. Note that when the checkbox is selected, the thresholding levels can be regulated only in the original channel. For example, selecting “Channel 1->2” will copy the ROI from channel 1 to channel 2.

The ROI generated in auto-mode will be stored as 

ROI files and can be reused if necessary. For this purpose, within the folder containing the analysed .ptu files, a new ROI folder will be created.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

All automatic-ROI variants operate on Foreground intensity. The channel controls expose the cell threshold, optional multiple-cell handling, ROI mode, object threshold and copy-from-other-channel option where applicable. Selecting another measurement rebuilds the candidates from that measurement’s foreground image, so an automatic mask must never be assumed to persist unchanged across files.

To correctly calculate concentration maps, the user must provide or import 

calibration data obtained from FCS measurements, including the focal volume width \omega_0, the structure parameter \kappa, and the mean molecular brightness.

Pressing the Calculate single button calculates and displays results for a single file. Press the Add to results button to save the results and retain the Auto ROI settings for the current file. The calculate all button will automatically calculate and store the data for all files, one by one.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

The GUI reports integrated values calculated from all reconstructed frames. Frame-resolved results are export-only and therefore do not add columns or controls to the visible GUI table. For every channel and frame, Phot2conc applies the same active ROI and reports foreground weighted counts, background weighted counts, molecule number, concentration and their corresponding uncertainty/statistical fields.

The mean result will be displayed in tables within the RESULTS window on the right-hand side of the screen

and presented in the form of per-pixel distributions for concentration, number of molecules - N_p, or number of photons, respectively.

The error values displayed in the RESULTS window can be calculated in two ways. The checkbox Errors as SEM switches between them:

In the first case (unmarked checkbox), the error is returned as the mean of the maximum errors calculated for each pixel. Those errors include errors for V_0 and the molecular brightness.

The second method for calculation of errors (marked checkbox) returns the standard error of the mean, calculated as the standard deviation SD over all pixels, divided by the square root of the number of pixels within the ROI or image (depending on whether the ROI is used or not).

During calculation, the data will be automatically exported according to the rules marked in the export panel.

For version v2.2.0 and higher:

Frame-resolved fields use one-based names of the form Frame_<N>_<metric>. Available metrics are <Counts>, Counts_std, <N_p>, N_p_err, <C>, C_err, C_median, C_median_abs_err, <Background counts> and Background_counts_std. Counts are TCSPC-weighted counts per pixel in the active ROI, N_p is molecules per pixel and C is concentration in nM. Frame 1 is the first reconstructed frame.

These columns are appended only to exported CSV, DAT or pickle tables. Fractional foreground/background counts are expected after statistical filtering because they are sums of event weights rather than raw photon counts. Older PKL files without frame products export only integrated fields.

The to array means that the script will create a .csv file containing the array (size of the image) containing a number of photons, molecules, or concentration in a given pixel.“to heatmap” means that the heatmap will be exported as the .png file.

To export the averaged data as a table, press the “Export all data” button.

The workflow for mapping the fluorophore’s concentration in living cells can be divided into two or three steps, depending on the user’s preferences.

Extract the information about photons from the binary .ptu file and filter the data to eliminate background or unwanted influence of autofluorescence or other fluorophores.

(OPTIONAL) Create the ROI file using external software, for example, ImageJ, to create a text image containing a selection of the pixels that should be included in the analysis. This step is optional because the third step offers automatic cell detection. Nevertheless, smICA nop includes a tool that translates the externally created ROI files to the format and structure understood by smICA. A detailed description of using the tool script can be found 

here. Roi Files can also be generated directly with smICA using the Auto ROI mode. The 

ROI mixer tool can be furter used to perform a product, sum, or subtract operations on as generated ROI files.

Calculate the map of the fluorophore concentration based on fluorescence intensity data and calibration data.

At the startup, the user can choose between two modes: 

EXTRACT from PTU and FILTER or 

Phot 2 Conc.

The first option is to extract raw data from the .ptu files, filter the data using time gating, or apply statistical filters based on the fluorescence decay pattern. The second option provides a GUI for mapping the concentration of fluorescent molecules within living cells. Below is a detailed description of each mode.
You can also switch between modes by selecting the proper option from the Mode menu.



For version v2.2.0 and higher:

The analysis can be performed interactively or reproduced through the local TCP interface. In extraction mode, configure the gate and accepted statistical filters once and use the native Apply to all callback. In Phot2conc, configure calibration and ROI selection and use the native Calculate all callback. These callbacks keep the normal GUI progress window active.

Long workflows may retain a resume-state file. The completed extraction or calculation batches are skipped after a restart. The workflow report records status, counts of processed and reused data, elapsed time, and machine information. File-based ROI analysis enumerates all ROIs that match the selected measurement, rather than assuming only ROI_0.

The start screen remains the entry point for interactive analysis. Tests installed with smICA can be executed separately with run_smICA --test on Linux or smICA.bat --test on Windows. Test mode does not initialize the GUI and presents explicit expected and calculated numerical values for every comparison.
